tip: 'Recht haben' means 'to be right' – literally 'to have right'.
'Excited about' is 'begeistert von' in German, not 'über': 'begeistert von der neuen Ausstellung'.
'Einfluss' pairs with 'auf' plus the accusative: 'Einfluss auf die Entscheidung'.
Use 'um' for clock times: 'um acht Uhr' = at eight o'clock.
Separable verb 'ankommen' splits: the prefix 'an' jumps to the end, as in 'kam heute an'.
'Von' always takes the dative, so 'eine' becomes 'einer': 'träumst von einer Weltreise'.
German uses the present with 'seit' for ongoing time: 'wohnen seit fünf Jahren' = have been living for five years.
'Will' means 'wants to', not English 'will': 'will die Lavaproben analysieren' = wants to analyze the lava samples.
'Die Lehrerin' – feminine. The '-in' ending makes professions feminine.
'Welpe' is one of the nouns that add '-n' when not the subject: 'den Welpen'.
'Die Blume' – feminine. '-e' ending often signals feminine gender.
Separable verbs normally put 'ge' in the middle in the perfect: 'aufhören' becomes 'aufgehört'.
The 'du' command of 'aufpassen' drops the ending and splits: 'pass ... auf'.
'Viertel nach' means 'quarter past': 'Viertel nach sieben' is 7:15.
'Ob' (whether) introduces an indirect yes/no question, and the verb moves to the end: 'ob das richtig ist'.
Before an uncountable noun, 'viel' usually takes no ending: 'viel Eisen'.
'Zum ersten Mal' is the fixed phrase for 'for the first time'.
'Lust haben' means 'to feel like' – 'Hast du Lust?' is a casual invitation.
For body parts German uses 'sich' plus the article, not a word for 'his': 'putzt sich ... die Zähne' = brushes his teeth.
Months take 'im': 'im März' = in March.
German says the ones before the tens: 'fünfundvierzig' is literally five-and-forty (45).
For a masculine direct object 'ein' becomes 'einen': 'einen Wintermantel'.
'Wegen' (because of) normally takes the genitive: 'wegen Bauarbeiten'.
For a masculine direct object 'dieser' becomes 'diesen': 'diesen schwarzen Pullover'.
The idiom 'fünf gerade sein lassen' (here with 'zu') is literally 'let five be an even number': accept small wrongness instead of correcting everything.
German often uses the 24-hour clock: 'neunzehn Uhr' = 7 p.m.
English 'not a single' is normally 'kein einziges', not 'nicht ein': 'kein einziges günstiges Hotelzimmer'.
Formal commands put the verb first, then 'Sie': 'Entschuldigen Sie' means 'excuse me', addressed politely.
To negate a whole noun, German uses 'kein' instead of 'nicht': 'keine Hilfe' means no help.
The 'du' command drops '-st', the pronoun, and here the umlaut: 'du schläfst' becomes just 'schlaf'.
